technique: entering mid-action, with no setup at all
lesson:
Today we work on one technique: starting a poem in the middle of something, with no introduction. The poet gives you no title scene, no "it was morning," no explaining. The poem just starts inside a thing already happening.

Look at the first word: "Woodsmoke first." That is a smell, handed to you before you know where you are. Then "Then the sweeter rot: wet leaf." You are moving through smells and the year already in progress. By "a dead tree you took down yesterday," you are in the middle of a day's work with no setup at all.

It works because you have to catch up. Starting in the middle makes you pay attention right away, because you want to know where you are.

Try this: cut your first two sentences of explaining. Start on the third, inside the action.

The second time through, listen for how the whole poem builds toward the last words, "So — up!"

Here is the poem.
poem:
Woodsmoke first—somebody's chimney two hills over,
or your own from last night, settled into wool and skin,
the smell of burning that means the year has turned its back
on warmth and means it. Then the sweeter rot: wet leaf,
the apple no one picked gone soft against the root,
a dead tree you took down yesterday still pale at the cut,
sound all the way through, good for standing in the ground
a few years yet. That's honest math—a post that won't
outlast you, set deep anyway, tamped on stone by hand.
The light finds the frost on everything and burns it off slow.
There's a line you've been meaning to draw out there, wild
on one side, yours on the other, and nothing draws it but you.

Posts in the ground, a fence taking shape, a line between what's wild and what you're making—that work only happens with your hands on it,

So — up!
